questions.stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that

options.text: the two alleles of a gene separate during the formation of gametes
dominant alleles are always more common than recessive alleles
all offspring resemble the dominant parent
alleles of different genes are always inherited together

questions.explanation: Because homologous chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles during meiosis I, the two alleles at any locus end up in different gametes. Each gamete therefore carries only one allele of each gene, which is why a Tt parent produces T and t gametes in equal numbers.

distractorRationale.b: Dominance describes how an allele is expressed, not how common it is in a population
distractorRationale.c: A heterozygous cross produces some offspring with the recessive phenotype
distractorRationale.d: Independent assortment says the opposite for genes on different chromosomes

questions.stem: A homozygous tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a homozygous dwarf plant (tt). What are the offspring?
questions.explanation: Every gamete from the TT parent carries T and every gamete from the tt parent carries t, so all offspring are Tt. Since T is dominant they all look tall, but each carries a hidden recessive allele.

distractorRationale.a: The recessive allele is masked by the dominant T in every offspring
distractorRationale.c: A 1 : 1 ratio results from Tt crossed with tt, not from TT crossed with tt
distractorRationale.d: A 3 : 1 ratio results from crossing two heterozygotes

questions.stem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants are crossed (Tt × Tt). What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?
questions.explanation: Each parent produces T and t gametes equally, so the four possible combinations are TT, Tt, Tt and tt. Three of these contain at least one dominant T and are therefore tall, giving the classic 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio, while the underlying genotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.

distractorRationale.a: A 1 : 1 ratio comes from a test cross, Tt × tt
distractorRationale.c: One quarter of the offspring inherit t from both parents and are dwarf
distractorRationale.d: An intermediate phenotype would require incomplete dominance, which does not apply to pea height

questions.stem: A farmer has a tall pea plant but does not know whether it is TT or Tt. Which cross would settle the question, and how?

options.text: Cross it with a TT plant; dwarf offspring would show it is Tt
Cross it with a dwarf (tt) plant; any dwarf offspring would show it is Tt
Cross it with another tall plant of unknown genotype; the ratio will always be 3 : 1
Examine the plant's leaves under a microscope

questions.explanation: In a test cross the tt partner contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring reveal what the unknown parent contributed. If it is TT every offspring is Tt and tall; if it is Tt then half receive t from both parents and are dwarf, so even one dwarf offspring proves it is heterozygous.

distractorRationale.a: A TT partner masks everything, since every offspring inherits at least one T and is tall
distractorRationale.c: The ratio depends on both parents' genotypes, so an unknown partner gives an ambiguous result
distractorRationale.d: Genotype cannot be read from leaf appearance under a microscope

questions.stem: In a certain plant, red flower colour (R) is dominant to white (r). A cross between a heterozygous red plant and a white plant produces 60 offspring. Approximately how many are expected to be white?
questions.explanation: The cross is Rr × rr, which gives offspring in the ratio 1 Rr : 1 rr, so half are expected to be white. Half of 60 is 30. Note that this test cross gives a 1 : 1 ratio rather than the 3 : 1 of a heterozygous self-cross.

distractorRationale.a: 15 would be a quarter, which is the white proportion in an Rr × Rr cross
distractorRationale.b: 20 would be a third, which no monohybrid cross produces
distractorRationale.d: 45 is three quarters, the proportion that would be red in an Rr × Rr cross

questions.stem: In the four o'clock plant, a red-flowered plant crossed with a white-flowered plant gives all pink offspring, and crossing two pink plants gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. This pattern is called
questions.explanation: Under incomplete dominance neither allele fully masks the other, so the heterozygote has its own intermediate phenotype. Because all three genotypes now look different, the phenotypic ratio matches the genotypic ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 instead of collapsing to 3 : 1.

distractorRationale.a: Complete dominance would make the heterozygote indistinguishable from the dominant homozygote, giving 3 : 1
distractorRationale.c: Sex linkage concerns genes on the sex chromosomes and gives different results in males and females
distractorRationale.d: Independent assortment concerns the inheritance of two or more different genes

questions.stem: Two dwarf pea plants (tt) are crossed. What proportion of the offspring will be tall?
questions.explanation: Neither parent carries the dominant T allele, so no gamete can supply one and every offspring must be tt. A recessive characteristic breeds true, which is why homozygous recessive lines are so useful in test crosses.

distractorRationale.b: A quarter would require both parents to carry a hidden T allele
distractorRationale.c: A half would require one parent to be heterozygous
distractorRationale.d: Three quarters is the tall proportion in a Tt × Tt cross

questions.stem: If a cross predicts a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio, then in any family of four offspring exactly three must show the dominant characteristic.
questions.explanation: False. A 3 : 1 ratio expresses the probability for each individual offspring, three chances in four. Just as four coin tosses can all give heads, all four offspring could show the dominant characteristic; the ratio is only approached reliably in large numbers, which is why Mendel counted thousands of plants.

questions.stem: Two pea plants, both tall, are crossed and among their offspring a dwarf plant appears. What must the genotypes of the two parents have been?
questions.explanation: A dwarf plant is tt, so it received a recessive t allele from each parent, meaning both parents must carry t. Since both parents are tall they must each also carry T, so both were heterozygous Tt.

distractorRationale.a: Neither parent would carry a t allele, so no dwarf offspring could arise
distractorRationale.b: Only one parent could contribute t, and the other would always contribute T, so all offspring would be tall
distractorRationale.d: A tt parent would be dwarf, but the question states both parents were tall

questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black coat colour (B) is dominant to white (b). Using a Punnett square, work out the genotypic and phenotypic ratios expected when two heterozygous black guinea pigs are crossed. State Mendel's law that explains why each parent produces two kinds of gamete.
markingGuide: Symbols defined: B is the allele for black, b the allele for white, B dominant to b (1 mark)
Parental genotypes correctly stated as Bb and Bb, both black in phenotype (2 marks)
Gametes correctly shown: each parent produces B and b in equal proportion (2 marks)
Punnett square drawn and correctly filled with BB, Bb, Bb and bb (3 marks)
Genotypic ratio stated as 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb (1 mark)
Phenotypic ratio stated as 3 black : 1 white (1 mark)
Law of segregation stated: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one of them (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The cross gives a genotypic ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 and a phenotypic ratio of 3 black : 1 white, because BB and Bb both appear black while only bb is white. The law of segregation is what guarantees the two kinds of gamete, since the homologous chromosomes carrying B and b are separated in meiosis I.

questions.stem: According to Mendel's law of independent assortment, the inheritance of one trait does not affect the inheritance of another trait. Which of the following scenarios exemplifies this law?

options.text: A dihybrid cross between two pea plants with different traits.
A monohybrid cross between two homozygous plants.
A test cross involving a homozygous recessive plant.
A cross between two plants with the same phenotype.

questions.explanation: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that alleles for different traits segregate independently of each other during gamete formation. A dihybrid cross is a classic example of this law, where two traits are considered and their inheritance patterns are analyzed independently.

distractorRationale.b: A monohybrid cross only involves one trait and does not demonstrate independent assortment.
distractorRationale.c: A test cross does not involve multiple traits and is used primarily to determine the genotype of an organism.
distractorRationale.d: Crossing plants with the same phenotype does not provide information about the independent assortment of traits.

questions.stem: In a Punnett square, what does each box represent?

options.text: A possible genotype of the offspring.

questions.explanation: Each box in a Punnett square represents a possible genotype of the offspring resulting from the combination of alleles from the parents. This tool helps visualize the genetic makeup of potential offspring.

distractorRationale.b: The phenotype of the parents is not directly represented in the boxes of the Punnett square.
distractorRationale.c: The Punnett square does not indicate the number of offspring, but rather the potential genetic combinations.
distractorRationale.d: The boxes show all possible genotypes, not just the dominant trait.

questions.stem: If a plant with genotype AaBb is crossed with another plant with genotype Aabb, what will be the phenotypic ratio of the offspring?
questions.explanation: The cross between AaBb and Aabb will yield four different combinations of phenotypes among the offspring, leading to a 1:1:1:1 ratio of the different phenotypes. This is typical of a dihybrid cross involving a heterozygous and a homozygous recessive parent.

distractorRationale.a: The 3:1 ratio applies to monohybrid crosses, not to this dihybrid scenario.
distractorRationale.c: The 1:2:1 ratio is characteristic of a monohybrid cross, not applicable here.
distractorRationale.d: The 9:3:3:1 ratio applies to a typical dihybrid cross between two heterozygotes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a test cross?

options.text: Crossing a homozygous dominant with a homozygous recessive.
Crossing an unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive.

questions.explanation: A test cross is performed by crossing an individual with an unknown genotype, typically heterozygous, with a homozygous recessive individual. This allows the determination of the unknown genotype based on the phenotypic ratios of the offspring.

distractorRationale.a: Crossing two homozygous individuals does not help determine unknown genotypes.
distractorRationale.b: Crossing a homozygous dominant with a homozygous recessive only shows dominant traits.
distractorRationale.d: Crossing two heterozygous individuals does not reveal the genotype of one of the parents.

questions.stem: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals (Tt), what is the expected genotypic ratio of the offspring?
questions.explanation: The expected genotypic ratio from a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals (Tt x Tt) is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, which simplifies to a 1:2:1 ratio. This reflects the different combinations of alleles that can occur.

distractorRationale.b: The 3:1 ratio refers to phenotypes, not genotypes.
distractorRationale.c: The 2:1 ratio is not applicable in a simple monohybrid cross.
distractorRationale.d: The 1:1 ratio applies to a cross involving one homozygous and one heterozygous parent.

questions.stem: What is the phenotypic ratio expected from a monohybrid cross between a homozygous dominant and a homozygous recessive plant?
questions.explanation: In a monohybrid cross between a homozygous dominant (TT) and a homozygous recessive (tt) plant, all offspring will exhibit the dominant phenotype (Tt). Therefore, the phenotypic ratio is 100% dominant phenotype.

distractorRationale.a: A 1:1 ratio occurs in a different type of cross involving heterozygous and homozygous parents.
distractorRationale.b: The 3:1 ratio is characteristic of a cross between two heterozygous individuals.
distractorRationale.c: The 1:2:1 ratio applies to genotypes, not phenotypes in this case.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about Mendel's law of segregation?

options.text: All offspring will show the dominant trait.
Only dominant alleles are passed to offspring.

questions.explanation: Mendel's law of segregation states that during the formation of gametes, the two alleles for a trait segregate from each other so that each gamete carries only one allele for each gene. This principle is fundamental in understanding inheritance.

distractorRationale.b: Not all offspring will show the dominant trait; it depends on the genotypes involved.
distractorRationale.c: Homozygous individuals can produce gametes, each carrying one allele.
distractorRationale.d: Both dominant and recessive alleles can be passed to offspring depending on the parent's genotype.

questions.stem: If a plant with the genotype AABb is crossed with a plant with the genotype AaBb, what is the probability of obtaining an offspring with the genotype AaBb?
questions.explanation: To determine the probability of obtaining the genotype AaBb from the cross AABb x AaBb, we can use a Punnett square. The resulting combinations show that there are 4 possible combinations, with 2 resulting in AaBb, giving a probability of 1/2.

distractorRationale.a: 1/4 is too low for this cross; there are more combinations that yield AaBb.
distractorRationale.c: 3/8 does not accurately reflect the combinations from this cross.
distractorRationale.d: 1/8 is incorrect as it underestimates the combinations available.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of using a Punnett square in genetics?

options.text: To calculate the number of offspring.
To determine the environment's effect on traits.

questions.explanation: The primary purpose of using a Punnett square is to visualize the possible genetic combinations resulting from a genetic cross. It helps in predicting the likelihood of different genotypes and phenotypes in the offspring.

distractorRationale.b: The Punnett square does not calculate the number of offspring but rather the genetic outcomes.
distractorRationale.c: The Punnett square focuses on genetic inheritance, not environmental influences.
distractorRationale.d: Identifying mutations requires different techniques outside the scope of a Punnett square.

questions.stem: What is the expected phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals (Tt)?
questions.explanation: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals (Tt), the expected phenotypic ratio is 3:1. This means that out of four offspring, three will display the dominant trait and one will display the recessive trait.

distractorRationale.a: The ratio 1:2:1 represents the genotypic ratio, not the phenotypic ratio.
distractorRationale.c: The ratio 2:1 is not applicable in a simple monohybrid cross.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio 1:1 would occur in a test cross, not in a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals.

questions.stem: If a plant with genotype Aa is crossed with a homozygous recessive plant (aa), what is the probability of obtaining a homozygous dominant offspring?
questions.explanation: When a plant with genotype Aa is crossed with a homozygous recessive plant (aa), the possible offspring genotypes are Aa and aa. Therefore, there is a 0% probability of obtaining a homozygous dominant offspring (AA).

distractorRationale.b: 25% is the probability for a different cross, not applicable here.
distractorRationale.c: 50% is the probability for heterozygous offspring, not homozygous dominant.
distractorRationale.d: 100% cannot occur since homozygous dominant offspring cannot be produced in this cross.
